alternatives.root_cause: A checkout dependency (payment, cart/valkey, or email) became slow, and checkout failed because it waited on it.
alternatives.why_not: No downstream service raised any alert, and a dependency slow enough to time out checkout would normally show its own latency or error signal; still plausible if the dependency is unmonitored or if the slow hop is the cart's valkey store, which is absent from the graph.

alternatives.root_cause: A bad checkout release or a wrong config value (timeout, pool size, broker address) shipped just before onset.
alternatives.why_not: A broken artifact usually fails fast and loudly at startup rather than producing a minute of elevated latency before errors; the latency-then-error ramp fits saturation better.

verdict.summary: checkout exhausted an internal resource (connection/thread pool backing its many downstream calls), so requests queued until they timed out and order publication to Kafka stopped, starving accounting of traffic.
verdict.reasoning: The alert sequence is latency first, errors a minute later, then a downstream consumer going silent. That is the classic saturation shape: work arrives faster than it can be drained, queues grow, callers see slow then failed requests. checkout is the fan-out node here (product-catalog, currency, cart, email, payment, shipping), so it holds the most concurrent state and is the first to run out of workers or connections. Crucially, none of checkout's six dependencies alerted - no latency, no error-rate, no no-traffic alert on any of them - which argues the slowness originated inside checkout rather than being inherited from a slow or frozen dependency. accounting is absent from the call graph and alerts only on no-traffic, which fits an asynchronous order-event consumer downstream of checkout via Kafka: it broke because checkout stopped emitting orders, not on its own. I would not blame accounting, and frontend/frontend-proxy appear in the blast radius only by traversal.
open_questions: checkout's goroutine/thread, heap and connection-pool metrics around 00:51 - is there a saturation ramp preceding the first latency alert?
Per-dependency client latency histograms from checkout: did one callee's p99 move before checkout's own, which would flip this to dependency_latency?
Whether checkout's Kafka producer was erroring or blocking - a blocked producer send would both slow checkout and silence accounting, which is a distinct mechanism
Checkout deployment and config change history in the hour before onset (image tag, pool sizes, timeouts)
Request-rate trend into checkout: was there a traffic surge, which would make this capacity rather than a leak
